modules.title: Partitioning
modules.goal: Split large tables for pruning, maintenance and retention without breaking queries.

topics.title: Partitioning Basics
topics.simple: Partitioning table ko smaller pieces me todta hai.
topics.pro: A partitioned table routes rows into child partitions by a partition key, while queries use the parent name.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE enrollments_partitioned (student_id BIGINT, course_id INTEGER, enrolled_on DATE NOT NULL) PARTITION BY RANGE (enrolled_on);

topics.title: Range Partitioning
topics.simple: Range partition values ke intervals banata hai.
topics.pro: Range partitioning assigns rows to partitions based on value ranges such as months or years.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE enrollments_2026 PARTITION OF enrollments_partitioned FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-01-01') TO ('2027-01-01');

topics.title: List Partitioning
topics.simple: List partition discrete values ke liye hota hai.
topics.pro: List partitioning assigns rows to partitions by an explicit value list, such as region or status.
points: Each value belongs to one partition.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE students_in PARTITION OF students PARTITION BY LIST (region);

topics.title: Hash Partitioning
topics.simple: Hash partition rows ko evenly distribute karta hai.
topics.pro: Hash partitioning applies a hash to the key and routes rows to a fixed number of partitions.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE events_hash PARTITION OF events FOR VALUES WITH (MODULUS 4, REMAINDER 0);

topics.title: Partition Key
topics.simple: Partition key routing aur pruning decide karta hai.
topics.pro: The partition key determines which partition stores a row and which partitions a query can skip.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE events (id BIGINT, created_at DATE NOT NULL, payload JSONB) PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at);

topics.title: Partition Pruning
topics.simple: Pruning irrelevant partitions skip karta hai.
topics.pro: The planner prunes partitions whose bounds cannot match the query predicate, reducing scan work.
points: Use the partition key in predicates.

example.sql: EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM enrollments_partitioned WHERE enrolled_on >= '2026-01-01';
example.output: A plan touching only matching partitions.

topics.title: Creating Partitions
topics.simple: CREATE TABLE PARTITION OF child banata hai.
topics.pro: A partition is created with CREATE TABLE ... PARTITION OF parent FOR VALUES ... and inherits the parent columns.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE enrollments_2025 PARTITION OF enrollments_partitioned FOR VALUES FROM ('2025-01-01') TO ('2026-01-01');

topics.title: Attaching Partitions
topics.simple: Existing table ko partition attach kar sakte hain.
topics.pro: ATTACH PARTITION adds an existing table after validating its rows against the bounds.
points: Use CHECK constraints to speed validation.

example.sql: ALTER TABLE enrollments_partitioned ATTACH PARTITION enrollments_2025 FOR VALUES FROM ('2025-01-01') TO ('2026-01-01');

topics.title: Detaching Partitions
topics.simple: DETACH PARTITION partition ko parent se alag karta hai.
topics.pro: DETACH PARTITION removes a child from the partitioned table while keeping its data as a standalone table.

example.sql: ALTER TABLE enrollments_partitioned DETACH PARTITION enrollments_2025;

topics.title: Indexes on Partitions
topics.simple: Partitioned indexes parent par bhi bante hain.
topics.pro: Indexes created on the parent are propagated to partitions, and each child can also have its own indexes.

example.sql: CREATE INDEX enrollments_partitioned_student ON enrollments_partitioned (student_id);

topics.title: Constraints on Partitions
topics.simple: Partitioned tables constraints inherit karte hain.
topics.pro: CHECK, NOT NULL and foreign keys apply to partitions; unique constraints must include the partition key.

example.sql: ALTER TABLE enrollments_partitioned ADD PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_id, enrolled_on);

topics.title: Default Partition
topics.simple: Default partition unmatched rows ko catch karta hai.
topics.pro: A DEFAULT partition stores rows that match no other partition, preventing insert failures but hiding gaps.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE enrollments_default PARTITION OF enrollments_partitioned DEFAULT;

topics.title: Partition Maintenance
topics.simple: Old partitions detach aur archive karo.
topics.pro: Retention usually detaches or drops old partitions instead of running a huge DELETE.

example.sql: ALTER TABLE enrollments_partitioned DETACH PARTITION enrollments_2024;

topics.title: Partition vs Sharding
topics.simple: Partitioning ek database ke andar hota hai; sharding servers me.
topics.pro: Partitioning splits a table inside one PostgreSQL instance, while sharding distributes data across independent servers.

example.sql: -- Partitioning keeps one connection and one catalog

topics.title: Common Partition Errors
topics.simple: Overlapping bounds, missing key aur no pruning common errors hain.
topics.pro: Common failures are overlapping partition bounds, queries that do not filter the key, and unique constraints missing the partition key.
points: Include the key in unique constraints.

example.sql: SELECT * FROM enrollments_partitioned WHERE enrolled_on >= '2026-01-01' AND enrolled_on < '2027-01-01';

topics.title: Partition Performance
topics.simple: Partitioning scan kam karta hai, planning badha sakta hai.
topics.pro: Partitioning helps when queries prune and maintenance targets individual partitions, but too many partitions increase planning and catalog overhead.

example.sql: EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM enrollments_partitioned WHERE enrolled_on = '2026-05-01';

topics.title: Monitoring Partitions
topics.simple: Partition sizes aur row counts monitor karo.
topics.pro: Monitor child sizes and growth so retention and vacuum keep up with the workload.

example.sql: SELECT relname, reltuples FROM pg_class WHERE relname LIKE 'enrollments_%';

topics.title: Time Partitioning
topics.simple: Time-based range partitioning common pattern hai.
topics.pro: Monthly or yearly partitions make retention and time-range queries cheap.
points: Keep a default only as a safety net.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE events_2026_01 PARTITION OF events FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-01-01') TO ('2026-02-01');

topics.title: Subpartitioning
topics.simple: Partition ko further partition kar sakte hain.
topics.pro: A partition can itself be partitioned, enabling multi-level strategies such as year then region.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE events_2026 PARTITION OF events FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-01-01') TO ('2027-01-01') PARTITION BY LIST (region);

topics.title: Practical Partitioning
topics.simple: Partition key ko query pattern se choose karo.
topics.pro: Choose a key that appears in common filters and supports retention, then verify pruning with EXPLAIN.

example.sql: EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM events WHERE created_at >= '2026-01-01' AND created_at < '2026-02-01';

interview.q: Module 28 · Explain Partitioning Basics in a production query.
interview.answer: A partitioned table routes rows into child partitions by a partition key, while queries use the parent name. Key rules: The parent is logical. Partitions are physical. The key controls routing.

interview.q: Module 28 · Explain Range Partitioning in a production query.
interview.answer: Range partitioning assigns rows to partitions based on value ranges such as months or years. Key rules: Good for dates. Boundaries are explicit. A default partition catches gaps.

interview.q: Module 28 · Explain List Partitioning in a production query.
interview.answer: List partitioning assigns rows to partitions by an explicit value list, such as region or status. Key rules: Good for categories. Each value belongs to one partition. Unknown values need a default.

interview.q: Module 28 · Explain Hash Partitioning in a production query.
interview.answer: Hash partitioning applies a hash to the key and routes rows to a fixed number of partitions. Key rules: Good for even distribution. No natural range pruning. Choose a stable key.

interview.q: Module 28 · Explain Partition Key in a production query.
interview.answer: The partition key determines which partition stores a row and which partitions a query can skip. Key rules: Choose a common filter. Keep it immutable. Include it in primary keys.

interview.q: Module 28 · Explain Partition Pruning in a production query.
interview.answer: The planner prunes partitions whose bounds cannot match the query predicate, reducing scan work. Key rules: Use the partition key in predicates. Avoid functions on the key. Check EXPLAIN.

interview.q: Module 28 · Explain Creating Partitions in a production query.
interview.answer: A partition is created with CREATE TABLE ... PARTITION OF parent FOR VALUES ... and inherits the parent columns. Key rules: Create before inserting. Bounds must not overlap. Use a default partition carefully.

interview.q: Module 28 · Explain Attaching Partitions in a production query.
interview.answer: ATTACH PARTITION adds an existing table after validating its rows against the bounds. Key rules: Validate the data first. It can lock. Use CHECK constraints to speed validation.

interview.q: Module 28 · Explain Detaching Partitions in a production query.
interview.answer: DETACH PARTITION removes a child from the partitioned table while keeping its data as a standalone table. Key rules: It is useful for retention. CONCURRENTLY reduces locking. The table remains.

interview.q: Module 28 · Explain Indexes on Partitions in a production query.
interview.answer: Indexes created on the parent are propagated to partitions, and each child can also have its own indexes. Key rules: Create on the parent. Check child indexes. Unique indexes need the key.

interview.q: Module 28 · Explain Constraints on Partitions in a production query.
interview.answer: CHECK, NOT NULL and foreign keys apply to partitions; unique constraints must include the partition key. Key rules: Primary keys include the key. Foreign keys work per partition. Validation can be costly.

interview.q: Module 28 · Explain Default Partition in a production query.
interview.answer: A DEFAULT partition stores rows that match no other partition, preventing insert failures but hiding gaps. Key rules: It catches mistakes. It can grow large. Move rows before adding bounds.

interview.q: Module 28 · Explain Partition Maintenance in a production query.
interview.answer: Retention usually detaches or drops old partitions instead of running a huge DELETE. Key rules: Detach old data. Archive externally. Drop when safe.

interview.q: Module 28 · Explain Partition vs Sharding in a production query.
interview.answer: Partitioning splits a table inside one PostgreSQL instance, while sharding distributes data across independent servers. Key rules: Partitioning is local. Sharding is distributed. Both need a key.

interview.q: Module 28 · Explain Common Partition Errors in a production query.
interview.answer: Common failures are overlapping partition bounds, queries that do not filter the key, and unique constraints missing the partition key. Key rules: Keep bounds disjoint. Filter the key. Include the key in unique constraints.

interview.q: Module 28 · Explain Partition Performance in a production query.
interview.answer: Partitioning helps when queries prune and maintenance targets individual partitions, but too many partitions increase planning and catalog overhead. Key rules: Prune aggressively. Avoid hundreds of tiny partitions. Measure planning time.

interview.q: Module 28 · Explain Monitoring Partitions in a production query.
interview.answer: Monitor child sizes and growth so retention and vacuum keep up with the workload. Key rules: Check reltuples. Watch default partition growth. Automate new partitions.

interview.q: Module 28 · Explain Time Partitioning in a production query.
interview.answer: Monthly or yearly partitions make retention and time-range queries cheap. Key rules: Create future partitions. Detach old ones. Keep a default only as a safety net.

interview.q: Module 28 · Explain Subpartitioning in a production query.
interview.answer: A partition can itself be partitioned, enabling multi-level strategies such as year then region. Key rules: Use sparingly. More levels increase planning. Keep pruning keys aligned.

interview.q: Module 28 · Explain Practical Partitioning in a production query.
interview.answer: Choose a key that appears in common filters and supports retention, then verify pruning with EXPLAIN. Key rules: Match query filters. Plan retention. Test pruning. Monitor growth.

logic.answer: Retention usually detaches or drops old partitions instead of running a huge DELETE. Detach old data. Archive externally. Drop when safe.

logic.q: Module 28 · Why does Partition vs Sharding matter?
logic.answer: Partitioning splits a table inside one PostgreSQL instance, while sharding distributes data across independent servers. Partitioning is local. Sharding is distributed. Both need a key.

logic.q: Module 28 · Why does Common Partition Errors matter?
logic.answer: Common failures are overlapping partition bounds, queries that do not filter the key, and unique constraints missing the partition key. Keep bounds disjoint. Filter the key. Include the key in unique constraints.

debug.title: Overlapping bounds
debug.broken:
CREATE TABLE p1 PARTITION OF events FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-01-01') TO ('2026-07-01');
CREATE TABLE p2 PARTITION OF events FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-06-01') TO ('2027-01-01');
debug.fix: CREATE TABLE p2 PARTITION OF events FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-07-01') TO ('2027-01-01');

debug.title: No partition for row
debug.fix: CREATE TABLE events_2028 PARTITION OF events FOR VALUES FROM ('2028-01-01') TO ('2029-01-01');
debug.error: no partition of relation "events" found for row

debug.title: Unique key missing partition column
debug.broken: ALTER TABLE events ADD PRIMARY KEY (id);
debug.fix: ALTER TABLE events ADD PRIMARY KEY (id, created_at);
debug.error: unique constraint on partitioned table must include all partition key columns

debug.title: Function blocks pruning
debug.broken: EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM events WHERE DATE_TRUNC('month', created_at) = '2026-01-01';
debug.fix: EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM events WHERE created_at >= '2026-01-01' AND created_at < '2026-02-01';
debug.error: The function on the key prevents partition pruning

debug.title: Default partition growth
debug.broken: CREATE TABLE events_default PARTITION OF events DEFAULT;
debug.fix: Create explicit partitions for expected ranges and keep the default as a temporary safety net.
debug.error: The default partition accumulates unexpected rows

debug.title: Attach without validation
debug.broken: ALTER TABLE events ATTACH PARTITION old_events FOR VALUES FROM ('2024-01-01') TO ('2025-01-01');
debug.fix:
ALTER TABLE old_events ADD CONSTRAINT old_events_check CHECK (created_at >= '2024-01-01' AND created_at < '2025-01-01');
ALTER TABLE events ATTACH PARTITION old_events FOR VALUES FROM ('2024-01-01') TO ('2025-01-01');
debug.error: The attach scans and locks to validate rows

debug.title: Detach missing partition
debug.broken: ALTER TABLE events DETACH PARTITION events_2024;
debug.fix: ALTER TABLE events DETACH PARTITION events_2024 CONCURRENTLY;
debug.error: A normal detach can block concurrent work

debug.title: Query misses key
debug.fix: SELECT * FROM events WHERE id = 1 AND created_at >= '2026-01-01';

debug.title: Too many partitions
debug.broken: CREATE TABLE events_2026_01_01 PARTITION OF events FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-01-01') TO ('2026-01-02');
debug.fix: Use monthly partitions instead of daily partitions unless the workload truly needs daily pruning.

debug.title: Drop parent
debug.error: cannot drop table events because other objects depend on it
debug.expected: The partitioned table and children are removed.
